claims.text: Overall phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the development of short-range chemical order.
Retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness follows from SRO-governed phase stability.
An optimal Al content promotes local chemical ordering within a single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni matrix.
Local chemical ordering minimizes free-energy fluctuations and stabilizes the phases.
Increasing or decreasing Al away from the optimal composition reduces SRO.
Reduced SRO destabilizes the phase and degrades the targeted properties.
The initial alloy can be made nearly single-phase and endowed with inherent SRO by homogenization annealing and selection of an optimal Al content.
Slightly increasing or decreasing Al from the optimum provides a controlled compositional perturbation expected to reduce SRO.
The degree of SRO is measurable by diffuse scattering or anomalous X-ray scattering.
Optimal Al content induces local chemical ordering that reduces free-energy fluctuations.
Reduced free-energy fluctuations stabilize the alloy phase and lock in the performance-supporting microstructure.
Diminished SRO causes microstructural instability and consequent performance degradation.
The optimal-Al alloy will exhibit higher SRO intensity than alloys with slightly modified Al content.
The optimal-Al alloy will show greater phase stability than the compositionally modified alloys.
The optimal-Al alloy will have superior high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the modified-Al alloys.
The hypothesis is limited primarily to single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys processed to promote SRO and excludes extreme processing, multiphase segregation, and non-equilibrium cooling.
The quantitative relationships between SRO intensity and toughness, radiation tolerance, and the other individual properties are not fully established.
Grain size and defect density may also influence the measured properties.

Failure of modified-Al alloys to show a statistically significant SRO reduction, or failure of reduced SRO to correlate consistently with lower phase stability and performance, is designated as a falsifying result.
